newsitem.title: UK: Physical cocoa - Buyers are in charge.
newsitem.headline: Physical cocoa - Buyers are in charge.

text.p: Cocoa buyers are in no hurry to top up existing stocks, relying on a comfortable flow of West African supply despite some concerns about dry weather.
"At the moment there seems to be plenty of stocks around, nobody is panicking too much," said one physical cocoa trader.
"All the buyers went to the woods. Sellers are too expensive. There is no activity, except the odd nearby stuff," said another.
Industry buyers are taking comfort in the fact that West African arrivals already point to a large crop, and unless they taper off quickly the harvest may approach last year's record.

They were not taking much notice of crop prospects in Brazil, which according to trade house E.D.&F. Man is likely to produce the smallest crop for almost 30 years unless rainfall increases, and in Indonesia where output growth is perceived to be slowing.
Analysts are contemplating an Ivorian crop of at least one million tonnes in 1996/97 based on 900,000 tonnes already gathered and weekly arrivals now running at around 20,000-25,000 tonnes.
But some experts say there is no reason to be too complacent as the midcrop can still hold a few surprises when it begins at end-April.
Temperatures have risen unusually in February and prolonged dryness can slash the prospects for the midcrop, which last year reached a hefty 200,000 tonnes.
"The weather in February has not been favourable to the crop development but that doesn't necessarily mean that it's going to be detrimental because March is quite crucial as well," said one analyst.
"But certainly we would need a significant improvement in weather in March to maintain that crop," he added.
Rains spread inland from coastal Ivorian cocoa areas this week after February drought, but analysts say heavier rainfalls will be needed for a good midcrop growth.
The midcrop is key since it may determine whether the 1996/97 harvest is in line with goverment projections of 950,000 tonnes or close to 1.1 million as many analysts suggest.
Man cocoa has forecast the midcrop at 150,000 tonnes depending on favourable weather in February and March.
Physical business was dormant this week with the only trade reported to be an Ivorian March shipment at 12 stg under LIFFE futures. February was being offered at 40 stg under May.
Ghana offers have also dried up after some 20,000 tonnes sold last week. The premium on Ghana has disappeared and bids were around 15-20 stg for April-June under London futures.
One reason for slackened demand was lack of interest for European liquid butter, traders said.
But another setback was a perception that Ivorian shippers were holding back cocoa in warehouses, although they may have deblocked them for shipment, to tap higher prices.
"All the shippers are taking a punt against the market, it's creating a lot of unrest," said one trader, blaming the automated marketing system for creating the backlog.
"The market knows that when the market rallies it should be sold immediately because there are so many longs in Ivory Coast," he added.
